# Market Incident Response — Cultural Misjudgement in Campaign [X], Market [Y]
## Recommendation for the Crisis Group

**Version 0.9 — draft for decision. Prepared for the crisis group, and for simultaneous release to the market leadership team in [Y]. Not for external circulation, not for the wider marketing function, and specifically not for the agency of record until §7.2 has been settled.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

This document assumes something the group may wish to contest before reading further: that the fastest available response is not the same thing as the best one, and that the gap between them is roughly six hours. Almost everything expensive about incidents of this kind is decided inside that window, usually by whoever is awake.

We would therefore ask two courtesies before this travels.

First, that the market managing director and the [Y] communications lead see §§4, 6 and 7 **before** the group takes a position, and have room to respond in their own terms. A response to a local cultural misjudgement that is drafted centrally and delivered to the market as a finished artefact has already repeated the error that caused the incident. Colleagues in [Y] will notice that before they notice the apology, and so, eventually, will everyone else.

Second, that §11 (legal, regulatory and platform gates) be walked with Group Legal and local counsel before any statement is published anywhere. The most common single cause of a second news cycle is a well-intentioned apology that concedes a fact local regulators had not yet established, or that reaches a distributor after it reaches their customers.

Section 3 is a diagnosis, not a formality. We would rather spend four hours on it than four months on the consequences of skipping it. If the group's judgement is that we do not have four hours, §2 lists what can be done immediately without any diagnosis at all, and none of it forecloses a later choice.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Withdraw globally and immediately; apologise locally, specifically, in language, from a named local human, within 24 hours; devolve the response to the market with a bounded and publicly conferred mandate; resist the instinct to buy reputation back with advertising; and convert the incident into a checkable structural change in who holds creative sign-off — published at 90 days whether or not anyone is still asking.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Immediate, non-negotiable | Campaign withdrawn in **all** markets, not only [Y]; paid amplification killed; scheduled social frozen network-wide; legal hold on all creative development records (§2) |
| Response posture | To be set at §4 by the crisis group, from four defined options. Our recommendation: **Posture 2 — Withdraw and Apologise** — subject to the §3 diagnosis not revealing orchestration |
| Who speaks | The **most senior [Y]-based executive**, in [local language], in local media and local channels. Not the Group CEO. Not the CMO. Not a logo on a grey square |
| Who decides | The **[Y] market MD**, under a written, bounded, time-limited mandate conferred visibly by the Group CEO (§7.1) |
| The centre's own binding | The centre may override a market decision, but must give written reasons **to the same audience that saw the decision**, and overrides are logged and reported to the board (§7.3) |
| Sequencing rule | Employees first. Then partners and trade. Then regulators. Then affected-community interlocutors. Then media. Global markets last and quietly (§6) |
| Principal risk | Not the original offence — the **second cycle**, generated by our own response. Roughly two-thirds of durable damage in comparable incidents accrues after the first apology, not before it *(judgement — §15)* |
| Restoration mechanism | Structural, checkable, and boring: local creative authority, a standing local review panel with teeth, and one long-horizon commitment in [Y] with no brand marks on it (§9) |
| What we will not do | Buy influencers, seed comments, delete criticism, litigate against critics, or publish a "learning journey" (§13) |
| Numeric failure test | If at T+30 days negative volume has not decayed to <20% of peak **and** trade partners have not reversed withdrawal decisions, the response has failed; escalate to §12.4 rather than repeating it louder |
| Investment sought | **$2.4M** immediate response envelope; **$6.8M** twelve-month restoration (illustrative, assumptions at §14.1) |
| Decisions requested | **Four** — §14.4, sought at the crisis group session at **T+6 hours** |
| Owner | Group Chief Communications Officer accountable; **[Y] market MD executing**; incident director named within 2 hours of approval |

### 1.1 The proposition, and how confident we are in it

An audience does not forgive a brand for being sorry. It forgives a brand for becoming *predictable again* — and predictability is demonstrated by conduct over weeks, not by language in the first 24 hours. The apology's only real job is to buy the standing to be judged on conduct.

*(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a measured finding. The evidence key at §15 marks which statements in this document are which. The group is entitled to know where we are reasoning and where we are reporting.)*

---

## 2. The first four hours — moves that require no diagnosis

These foreclose nothing. They can be executed by the incident director on standing authority and should not wait for the crisis group to convene.

| # | Action | Owner | By |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pull the creative from every paid channel, **every market** | Global media lead | T+1h |
| 2 | Freeze all scheduled brand social globally, including unrelated content and other brands in the house | Social ops | T+1h |
| 3 | Remove the asset from owned properties; do **not** delete audience comments, and record that we did not | Digital | T+2h |
| 4 | Legal hold: briefs, approval chains, agency correspondence, research, translations, any local objection raised and overridden | Group Legal | T+2h |
| 5 | Holding line, one paragraph, published in [local language] first: *we have withdrawn it, we are listening, a fuller response follows within 24 hours from [named person]* | [Y] comms lead | T+3h |
| 6 | Brief customer-facing and retail staff in [Y] **before** any public statement — script, permission to acknowledge, escalation route, and explicit safety guidance | [Y] HR + ops | T+3h |
| 7 | Notify the top trade partners and distributors in [Y] by phone, not email | [Y] commercial lead | T+4h |
| 8 | Stand up listening: local-language monitoring, not English-language monitoring of a non-English market | Insight | T+2h |
| 9 | Freeze all campaign work in the region pending §9.2 | Regional CMO | T+4h |

**Note on #5.** The holding line commits to a time and a named person. That is deliberate. A holding statement that commits to nothing reads as a legal artefact and is treated as one.

**Note on #3.** Comment deletion is recoverable in exactly no cases and has ended several careers that the original creative would not have. We would ask that this be stated to the digital team as an instruction rather than a preference.

---

## 3. Diagnosis before design — four hours, run in parallel with §2

We would gently ask the group to test one framing before adopting it. The incident is currently described as *a cultural misunderstanding*. The evidence available to us may instead describe **a governance failure wearing cultural clothing** — and only one of those is fixed by an apology.

### 3.1 The three questions that change the response

**Q1 — Was there local objection, and was it overridden?**
Check the approval chain now, before anyone tidies it. If someone in [Y] flagged this and was overruled by the centre or by the agency, the story is no longer about a joke. It is about a company that does not listen to its own people, which is a considerably more durable and more damaging narrative — and one that will surface, because the person who raised the flag has a phone.

*If the answer is yes:* the apology must acknowledge the override without naming or exposing the individual, and §9.3 (structural remedy) moves from Month 3 to Week 2. Attempting to conceal it is the single highest-cost option available.

**Q2 — Who is actually offended, and in what proportion?**
Three distinguishable populations, easily conflated in a monitoring dashboard:

| Population | Signal | Response weight |
|---|---|---|
| Directly affected community in [Y] | Local-language, local platforms, community and religious/civic institutions, non-national-media | **Decisive** |
| Broadly sympathetic domestic public | Mainstream local media, general social | High |
| International commentary and diaspora | English-language, high volume, low local purchase | Moderate — real, but do not let it set the terms |
| Orchestrated or opportunistic actors | Coordinated timing, template language, competitor adjacency, political utility | See §4.3 |

The failure to separate these produces apologies pitched at the wrong audience — typically at international Twitter, in English, which reads in [Y] as further evidence that the market is an afterthought.

**Q3 — What exactly was the offence?**
Not "it was insensitive." Specifically: was it sacred/religious, ethnic or racial, historical or national-dignity, gender or family-role, class or caste, linguistic (a translation or transliteration error), or a matter of ritual propriety? These have materially different half-lives and materially different remedies. A translation error is repairable in a week; a perceived slight to national dignity can run for years and can attract state interest.

Have a local cultural interlocutor **outside the company** — not the agency, not an employee — describe the offence back to us in their own words within four hours. Then use *their* framing in the apology, not ours. This is the cheapest and most frequently skipped step in the entire response.

### 3.2 Severity classification

| Tier | Markers | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Local social irritation, no trade or regulator movement, decaying | Local correction, no global posture |
| 2 | National media, trade partners asking questions, government commentary absent | Posture 2, market-led (**most likely current state**) |
| 3 | Regulator or ministry engaged, retail delisting, boycott with an organised host, employee safety concerns | Posture 2 plus §12.4 escalation; Group CEO enters |
| 4 | Legal jeopardy, physical risk to staff, licence-to-operate threat | Separate protocol; this document is insufficient |

---

## 4. The calibration decision — four postures

We would ask the group to choose explicitly rather than to drift into one. Drift produces Posture 3 delivered with Posture 2 timing, which satisfies nobody.

| | Posture | When it fits | What it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Correct and continue** — fix the asset, brief note, no apology | Narrow technical error (mistranslation, wrong image credit), no dignity dimension, Tier 1 | Cheap. Fails badly if severity is misread |
| **2** | **Withdraw and apologise** — full withdrawal, unqualified apology, named accountability, structural remedy | Genuine offence to a real constituency, Tier 2–3. **Recommended** | High short-term visibility, lowest long-term cost |
| **3** | **Acknowledge and explain** — regret expressed, intent explained, asset withdrawn | Almost never. Explanation of intent reads universally as excuse | Usually generates the second cycle it seeks to avoid |
| **4** | **Hold** — withdraw quietly, decline to apologise | Genuine ambiguity **and** evidence of orchestration for commercial or political ends where concession invites escalation | High risk, occasionally correct, requires the group to accept a bad month deliberately |

### 4.1 Why we recommend Posture 2

The asymmetry is not close. An over-apology to an unoffended audience costs one news cycle and a mild internal embarrassment. An under-apology to a genuinely offended one costs a market position, and the second attempt is never believed. Given that asymmetry, we would apologise on the balance of probability rather than on proof.

### 4.2 The hedge to avoid at all costs

*"We are sorry if anyone was offended"* transfers the fault to the audience's sensitivity, is recognised as doing so in every language we are aware of, and has independently generated more coverage than the original creative in numerous comparable incidents *(judgement, though the pattern is well attested — §15)*. So has *"that was not our intent."* Intent is the brand's private property and no one else's concern. See §5.2.

### 4.3 The one circumstance in which we would counsel the group to hold its nerve

If the §3.1 Q2 analysis shows the reaction is substantially manufactured — coordinated timing, template language, a competitor or political actor with a clear interest, and **no independently locatable community objection** — then a full apology rewards the mechanism and reliably invites a repeat within the year.

We flag this not because we believe it is the current case (we do not, on present evidence), but because we would rather the group considered and rejected it in the next four hours than discovered it in six weeks. The test is falsifiable and cheap: can we find, in four hours, three credible local community or civic voices, unconnected to each other and to the campaign, who articulate the offence in their own terms? If yes, Posture 2, without further debate. If no, bring it back to the group before publishing.

---

## 5. The apology — architecture, not wording

Wording is the market's property (§7.1). Architecture is what we would ask to be fixed.

### 5.1 Eight components

| # | Component | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Name the offence in the offended community's own terms** | Taken from §3.1 Q3. Using their framing is the entire signal |
| 2 | **Unconditional regret** | No "if", no "any", no "may have" |
| 3 | **Named human accountability** | A senior [Y]-based person, by name and face. Corporate voice is the voice of an entity avoiding a person |
| 4 | **What has already been done** | Past tense, verifiable, ideally completed before publishing |
| 5 | **What will change in how decisions are made** | The only forward-looking element that carries weight |
| 6 | **A date** | A public commitment to report back at 90 days |
| 7 | **A route to be answered** | A monitored channel, in language, with a response commitment |
| 8 | **Nothing else** | No product mention. No values statement. No history of our community contribution. Each addition dilutes the whole |

### 5.2 The prohibited constructions

| Phrase pattern | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| "…if anyone was offended" | Conditional; blames the audience |
| "…was not our intention" | Irrelevant; heard as excuse |
| "…does not reflect who we are" | It does; it was approved by people who work here |
| "We have always celebrated diversity…" | Invites the receipts |
| "…a learning journey" | Frames harm as our development opportunity |
| "…the actions of an individual" | Scapegoating; sequel guaranteed |
| Passive voice for the offence, active voice for the remedy | Universally noticed |

### 5.3 Form and channel

Local language first and natively written — **not translated from an English original**, which is detectable and, in this specific context, itself part of the offence. Local platforms in [Y] before global platforms. Video is warmer than text and harder to quote out of context; a plain, unproduced, single-take piece to camera outperforms a produced statement *(judgement)*. No music. No brand furniture. No grey square.

**Timing:** within 24 hours of the incident being recognised, and not on a Friday evening local time, which is read everywhere as burial.

---

## 6. Sequencing — who hears it, in what order

Almost every avoidable injury in the next fortnight is a sequencing failure rather than a content failure.

| Order | Audience | Channel | By |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Y] employees, especially customer-facing and retail | Manager cascade, in person or by voice, with a script and permission to acknowledge | Before anything public |
| 2 | Employees globally | Internal note, brief, honest, no spin | T+6h |
| 3 | Trade partners, distributors, key retail accounts in [Y] | Named-person phone calls | T+8h |
| 4 | Regulators, relevant ministries, industry bodies in [Y] | Local counsel and government affairs, in the local convention | Before media |
| 5 | Affected-community interlocutors | Private, listening posture, **no cameras, no request for absolution** | T+12–24h |
| 6 | [Y] media and public | Statement per §5 | T+24h |
| 7 | International media | Reactive only. Point them to the local statement | On enquiry |
| 8 | Other markets | Quiet brief to market leads; no proactive global publication | T+36h |

**On #5.** The single most common error is to meet community representatives and photograph it. The meeting has value; the photograph converts it into a transaction and reliably offends the people it was intended to reassure. If a record is wanted, let the community party decide whether and how to describe it.

**On #8.** We would suggest the group resist the instinct to publish a global apology. In markets where the incident has not landed, a global statement creates the awareness it seeks to manage, and the coverage will be about the apology rather than about anything else. Contain the response geographically to the extent that platform reality permits, and be honest that it permits less than it used to.

---

## 7. Authority — who decides, and what the centre binds itself to

### 7.1 The market mandate

We recommend that the Group CEO confer, in writing and visibly, a **bounded mandate** on the [Y] market MD:

> *For the next 30 days, [name] decides the content, timing, language and channel of all communications relating to this incident in [Y], and the composition of the local remedy up to a value of $[1.5]M. They do not need to ask. Escalation to the crisis group is required only for the four reserved matters below. If you disagree with a decision they have taken, take it to them.*

**Reserved to the centre (four only):** legal admissions with cross

# Global Employee Empowerment & Adaptive Culture Initiative
## Guidance on Regional Leadership Adaptation — Recommendation for Sponsor Group

**Version 2.0 — complete. Prepared for sponsor group decision, and for prior circulation to the fourteen regional people leads. Not yet for employee communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note only, and then the substance.

This version differs from v1.0 in three ways that the reviewers were right to insist on. It now asks for specific decisions, with money and a date attached (§12). It answers the questions the first draft deferred — most importantly what the centre itself is bound by (§9). And the regional material has been re-cut so that no colleague opens it and finds their country described inside someone else's card.

The regional cards in §6 remain what they were: **working hypotheses, offered so that they can be corrected**. Where a region has its own diagnostic data, that data replaces the card and the card is retired for that unit (§5.4). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet taken place, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies we would ask the sponsor group to extend before this travels further. First, that the fourteen regional people leads and the four regional MDs see §§3, 4 and 9 and have time to respond in their own way before the board pack is assembled — a programme about devolved authority that arrives in a region fully formed has already contradicted itself, and colleagues will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §10 (consultation and legal gates) be walked through with Group Legal, the European Works Council secretariat and Group Reward before any part of this is described to employees anywhere. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches a works council after it reaches a newspaper, or reaches an employee before it reaches their own supervisor.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a thin global core and a wide local expression: four employee entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form process where a floor cannot lawfully or structurally be met; delivery method, language, sequencing and naming devolved entirely to regions; four instrumented pilots in Year 1 with a common measurement spine but deliberately different local design; and a published protocol binding the centre to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Global mandate | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — decision rights at the lowest competent level; an answered route for dissent; tolerance of good-faith error; employee-initiated internal movement. Each stated as a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to regions | Language, ritual, sequencing, symbolism, manager incentives, pace, communication channels, and the programme's name. We would suggest the centre resist standardising even the name |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one high-authority-distance, one low, one deskless-majority, one recently-acquired entity** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§7) |
| Principal risk | Middle-manager status and grade loss, not employee resistance (§8) |
| The centre's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the centre may reverse a devolved decision, but must give written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside regional metrics (§9) |
| Measurement | Within-region trend on four behavioural proxies weighted 70%, survey items 30%; acquiescence correction applied before any cross-region view is shown (§8.3) |
| Numeric failure test | Empowerment survey index +5 points or more while decision latency on the instrumented decision class improves <10% and internal-move rate is flat = declared failure, programme paused, no further capital (§8.5) |
| Investment sought | **$14.2M Year 1, $10.6M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions in §12.1), of which $6.9M is manager time relief — the line most often omitted and most often fatal |
| Funding split | Central P&L funds diagnostic, instrumentation, platform, central team and pilot facilitation; regions fund manager time with a **60% central offset in Y1, 30% in Y2, nil thereafter** (§12.3) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §12.5, sought at the sponsor group meeting on **18 March** |
| Programme owner | Group Chief People Officer, sponsor; named programme director recruited internally within 30 days of approval |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Empowerment mechanisms do not transfer between contexts; the conditions that make them work can be built in each. *(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a finding — see the evidence key at §14. We flag it because the sponsor group is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented in our own past programmes: exported behavioural vocabulary — "speak up", "own it", "disagree and commit" — produces regions that become fluent at the annual survey and unchanged on Tuesday morning. That outcome is worse than no initiative, because it consumes the credibility a second attempt would require.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before we design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the sponsor group to test

The initiative is currently described as culture change. The evidence available to us may instead describe a **decision-rights and information-flow** problem wearing culture-change clothing. Only one of those two responds to leadership behaviour work, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate driver | What leadership/empowerment training does to it |
|---|---|
| Decision rights formally held too high | Nothing — requires delegation-of-authority redesign |
| Rights delegated on paper, retracted in practice | Nothing until retraction is made visible and costly (§9) |
| Information does not reach the level holding authority | **Amplifies harm** — confident decisions on poor data |
| Managers lack coaching capability | Improves, *if* paired with funded time relief (§8.4) |
| Reward and grading pay for control, not for developing others | Nothing — the incentive wins every time (§8.2) |
| Employees have voice but no evidence it is ever acted on | Worsens — a further unanswered invitation deepens cynicism |
| Working-language barrier suppresses contribution | Nothing — needs channel design, not confidence-building (§11.1) |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Five weeks, no design freeze until it reports: 60 structured conversations across four organisational levels in eight countries (including two deskless-majority sites); an audit of the documented delegation-of-authority matrix against actual practice in twelve units; and a language-barrier check in the four sites where the working language is not the local one. Cost **$310K**.

If it finds that decision rights are formally too high, the largest part of the Year 2 training envelope should be redirected to delegation architecture and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, now answered rather than deferred

Will headquarters be bound by the same four entitlements? If regional colleagues discover that the centre reserves the right to overturn devolved decisions without giving reasons, the initiative becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. v1.0 left this open. **§9 now answers it with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism**, and we would ask the sponsor group to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what an employee is entitled to, not as how a manager must behave, so that very different conduct can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — decision rights sit at the lowest competent level
**Floor:** every employee can name the classes of decision they own and point to a recent instance of exercising one without seeking permission. *Competent* is doing real work in that sentence; this is not an argument for uniform flat structures.

### 3.2 Entitlement II — there is a route for dissent, and it is answered
**Floor:** every employee has at least one available channel through which they can contradict a superior's view **and receive a response**. The channel may be a written pre-read, a skip-level, a facilitated small group, a mentor, a shift huddle, or an anonymous board. It need never be a raised hand in a large meeting. The answered part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a statutory reporting channel. Disagreement about a business decision is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§10.3).

### 3.3 Entitlement III — good-faith error is absorbed, not attributed
**Floor:** within each unit, at least one specific, visible instance per quarter in which a good-faith mistake was absorbed rather than attributed, and the team can name it. Demonstrated, never announced. In several regions this must be framed collectively rather than individually to be usable at all (§6).

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — employees can initiate their own movement
**Floor (revised from v1.0):** an employee may apply for an internal role, project or rotation **without the incumbent manager holding a veto and without the manager being informed in advance of the application**.

v1.0 stated this as an absolute and was wrong to. In parts of the Gulf, mobility between entities is constrained by employer-tied work permits and is a legal matter, not a cultural one. In Japan, Korea and Taiwan, seniority-anchored career and reward structures make unrestricted lateral self-nomination structurally disruptive in ways that a global mandate cannot responsibly overrule from a distance. The floor above is the most we can hold everywhere; where even that cannot be met, §3.6 applies.

### 3.5 Everything else is regional property
Language, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, incentives, cadence, and the programme's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any region to refuse. A region that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to say what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, collective-agreement conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not discomfort) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | **Group Chief People Officer**, countersigned by the Regional MD and by Group Legal |
| Duration | **12 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in an internally published register, reviewed quarterly by the sponsor group |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless it is materially weaker than the floor. We expect four to eight across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general culture model

We would ask each region to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given mechanism functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Authority basis** | Does a manager's authority derive from role or from demonstrated expertise? | Whether devolution reads as trust or as abandonment |
| **Directness of disagreement** | Can dissent be public without cost to either party? | The design of the dissent channel (Entitlement II) |
| **Attribution of error** | Does a mistake attach to a person, a team, or a system? | Whether error tolerance can be individual or must be collective (III) |
| **Ambiguity tolerance** | Is an open brief experienced as freedom, or as information withheld? | How much structure must accompany autonomy |

### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. The functioning equivalent is a named, bounded, publicly conferred mandate: *"Priya decides this class of exception up to this threshold. She does not need to ask me. If you disagree with her, take it to her."* Our practitioner judgement is that this single act moves more behaviour than a quarter of workshops — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§14), and testable inside the pilots via the decision-latency proxy.

### 4.3 Sponsorship: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. The corrected position: the default stands, and a region wishing to depart from it does so through a **one-page note countersigned by the Regional MD and the programme director**, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner sponsor sits two or three levels below the Regional MD, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the senior figure as visible patron providing cover and air, the practitioner as the working engine. A junior sponsor without a senior patron will in several regions be read, reasonably, as the centre not taking the region seriously.

---

## 5. Using the regional cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 45 days. They describe patterns we have observed in workplaces, not peoples.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the gap likely sits · behaviour to add · behaviour to drop · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 60** · legal or structural watch item.

### 5.3 The 60-day indicator, and why it is on every card
The failure modes that matter most — courteous non-adoption, affirmative response with no movement — are precisely the ones you cannot detect by asking. Each card therefore names an observable proxy visible within 60 days.

The asymmetry is not close. An over-apology to an unoffended audience costs one news cycle and a mild internal embarrassment. ### 4.2 The working rule

> High authority distance and low disagreement-directness do not mean empowerment is unwelcome. They mean it must be **granted rather than seized** — granted visibly, specifically, bounded, and by someone whose authority the team already accepts.

In such contexts an open invitation ("bring me your ideas") is not empowerment; it is a test most colleagues will decline to sit. **Default:** regional sponsors are selected on observed practice — leaders whose own teams already exhibit the four entitlements — rather than on rank.

We acknowledged in v1.0 that this backfires in several regions, then handed the choice back, which was no recommendation at all. ## 3. Diagnosis before design — four hours, run in parallel with §2

We would gently ask the group to test one framing before adopting it. The incident is currently described as *a cultural misunderstanding*. The evidence available to us may instead describe **a governance failure wearing cultural clothing** — and only one of those is fixed by an apology.

### 3.1 The three questions that change the response

**Q1 — Was there local objection, and was it overridden?**
Check the approval chain now, before anyone tidies it. If someone in [Y] flagged this and was overruled by the centre or by the agency, the story is no longer about a joke. It is about a company that does not listen to its own people, which is a considerably more durable and more damaging narrative — and one that will surface, because the person who raised the flag has a phone.

*If the answer is yes:* the apology must acknowledge the override without naming or exposing the individual, and §9.3 (structural remedy) moves from Month 3 to Week 2. Attempting to conceal it is the single highest-cost option available.

**Q2 — Who is actually offended, and in what proportion?**
Three distinguishable populations, easily conflated in a monitoring dashboard:

| Population | Signal | Response weight |
|---|---|---|
| Directly affected community in [Y] | Local-language, local platforms, community and religious/civic institutions, non-national-media | **Decisive** |
| Broadly sympathetic domestic public | Mainstream local media, general social | High |
| International commentary and diaspora | English-language, high volume, low local purchase | Moderate — real, but do not let it set the terms |
| Orchestrated or opportunistic actors | Coordinated timing, template language, competitor adjacency, political utility | See §4.3 |

The failure to separate these produces apologies pitched at the wrong audience — typically at international Twitter, in English, which reads in [Y] as further evidence that the market is an afterthought.

**Q3 — What exactly was the offence?**
Not "it was insensitive." Specifically: was it sacred/religious, ethnic or racial, historical or national-dignity, gender or family-role, class or caste, linguistic (a translation or transliteration error), or a matter of ritual propriety? These have materially different half-lives and materially different remedies. A translation error is repairable in a week; a perceived slight to national dignity can run for years and can attract state interest.

Have a local cultural interlocutor **outside the company** — not the agency, not an employee — describe the offence back to us in their own words within four hours. Then use *their* framing in the apology, not ours. This is the cheapest and most frequently skipped step in the entire response.

| 2 | National media, trade partners asking questions, government commentary absent | Posture 2, market-led (**most likely current state**) |

## 4. The calibration decision — four postures

We would ask the group to choose explicitly rather than to drift into one. Drift produces Posture 3 delivered with Posture 2 timing, which satisfies nobody.

| | Posture | When it fits | What it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Correct and continue** — fix the asset, brief note, no apology | Narrow technical error (mistranslation, wrong image credit), no dignity dimension, Tier 1 | Cheap. Fails badly if severity is misread |
| **2** | **Withdraw and apologise** — full withdrawal, unqualified apology, named accountability, structural remedy | Genuine offence to a real constituency, Tier 2–3. **Recommended** | High short-term visibility, lowest long-term cost |
| **3** | **Acknowledge and explain** — regret expressed, intent explained, asset withdrawn | Almost never. Explanation of intent reads universally as excuse | Usually generates the second cycle it seeks to avoid |
| **4** | **Hold** — withdraw quietly, decline to apologise | Genuine ambiguity **and** evidence of orchestration for commercial or political ends where concession invites escalation | High risk, occasionally correct, requires the group to accept a bad month deliberately |

### 4.1 Why we recommend Posture 2

The asymmetry is not close. An over-apology to an unoffended audience costs one news cycle and a mild internal embarrassment. An under-apology to a genuinely offended one costs a market position, and the second attempt is never believed. Given that asymmetry, we would apologise on the balance of probability rather than on proof.

### 4.2 The hedge to avoid at all costs

*"We are sorry if anyone was offended"* transfers the fault to the audience's sensitivity, is recognised as doing so in every language we are aware of, and has independently generated more coverage than the original creative in numerous comparable incidents *(judgement, though the pattern is well attested — §15)*. So has *"that was not our intent."* Intent is the brand's private property and no one else's concern. See §5.2.

### 4.3 The one circumstance in which we would counsel the group to hold its nerve

If the §3.1 Q2 analysis shows the reaction is substantially manufactured — coordinated timing, template language, a competitor or political actor with a clear interest, and **no independently locatable community objection** — then a full apology rewards the mechanism and reliably invites a repeat within the year.

We flag this not because we believe it is the current case (we do not, on present evidence), but because we would rather the group considered and rejected it in the next four hours than discovered it in six weeks. The test is falsifiable and cheap: can we find, in four hours, three credible local community or civic voices, unconnected to each other and to the campaign, who articulate the offence in their own terms? If yes, Posture 2, without further debate. If no, bring it back to the group before publishing.

# Market Incident Response — Cultural Misjudgement in Campaign [X], Market [Y]
## Recommendation for the Crisis Group

**Version 0.9 — draft for decision. Prepared for the crisis group, and for simultaneous release to the market leadership team in [Y]. Not for external circulation, not for the wider marketing function, and specifically not for the agency of record until §7.2 has been settled.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

This document assumes something the group may wish to contest before reading further: that the fastest available response is not the same thing as the best one, and that the gap between them is roughly six hours. Almost everything expensive about incidents of this kind is decided inside that window, usually by whoever is awake.

We would therefore ask two courtesies before this travels.

First, that the market managing director and the [Y] communications lead see §§4, 6 and 7 **before** the group takes a position, and have room to respond in their own terms. A response to a local cultural misjudgement that is drafted centrally and delivered to the market as a finished artefact has already repeated the error that caused the incident. Colleagues in [Y] will notice that before they notice the apology, and so, eventually, will everyone else.

Second, that §11 (legal, regulatory and platform gates) be walked with Group Legal and local counsel before any statement is published anywhere. The most common single cause of a second news cycle is a well-intentioned apology that concedes a fact local regulators had not yet established, or that reaches a distributor after it reaches their customers.

Section 3 is a diagnosis, not a formality. We would rather spend four hours on it than four months on the consequences of skipping it. If the group's judgement is that we do not have four hours, §2 lists what can be done immediately without any diagnosis at all, and none of it forecloses a later choice.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Withdraw globally and immediately; apologise locally, specifically, in language, from a named local human, within 24 hours; devolve the response to the market with a bounded and publicly conferred mandate; resist the instinct to buy reputation back with advertising; and convert the incident into a checkable structural change in who holds creative sign-off — published at 90 days whether or not anyone is still asking.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Immediate, non-negotiable | Campaign withdrawn in **all** markets, not only [Y]; paid amplification killed; scheduled social frozen network-wide; legal hold on all creative development records (§2) |
| Response posture | To be set at §4 by the crisis group, from four defined options. Our recommendation: **Posture 2 — Withdraw and Apologise** — subject to the §3 diagnosis not revealing orchestration |
| Who speaks | The **most senior [Y]-based executive**, in [local language], in local media and local channels. Not the Group CEO. Not the CMO. Not a logo on a grey square |
| Who decides | The **[Y] market MD**, under a written, bounded, time-limited mandate conferred visibly by the Group CEO (§7.1) |
| The centre's own binding | The centre may override a market decision, but must give written reasons **to the same audience that saw the decision**, and overrides are logged and reported to the board (§7.3) |
| Sequencing rule | Employees first. Then partners and trade. Then regulators. Then affected-community interlocutors. Then media. Global markets last and quietly (§6) |
| Principal risk | Not the original offence — the **second cycle**, generated by our own response. Roughly two-thirds of durable damage in comparable incidents accrues after the first apology, not before it *(judgement — §15)* |
| Restoration mechanism | Structural, checkable, and boring: local creative authority, a standing local review panel with teeth, and one long-horizon commitment in [Y] with no brand marks on it (§9) |
| What we will not do | Buy influencers, seed comments, delete criticism, litigate against critics, or publish a "learning journey" (§13) |
| Numeric failure test | If at T+30 days negative volume has not decayed to <20% of peak **and** trade partners have not reversed withdrawal decisions, the response has failed; escalate to §12.4 rather than repeating it louder |
| Investment sought | **$2.4M** immediate response envelope; **$6.8M** twelve-month restoration (illustrative, assumptions at §14.1) |
| Decisions requested | **Four** — §14.4, sought at the crisis group session at **T+6 hours** |
| Owner | Group Chief Communications Officer accountable; **[Y] market MD executing**; incident director named within 2 hours of approval |

### 1.1 The proposition, and how confident we are in it

An audience does not forgive a brand for being sorry. It forgives a brand for becoming *predictable again* — and predictability is demonstrated by conduct over weeks, not by language in the first 24 hours. The apology's only real job is to buy the standing to be judged on conduct.

*(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience, not a measured finding. The evidence key at §15 marks which statements in this document are which. The group is entitled to know where we are reasoning and where we are reporting.)*

---

## 2. The first four hours — moves that require no diagnosis

These foreclose nothing. They can be executed by the incident director on standing authority and should not wait for the crisis group to convene.

| # | Action | Owner | By |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pull the creative from every paid channel, **every market** | Global media lead | T+1h |
| 2 | Freeze all scheduled brand social globally, including unrelated content and other brands in the house | Social ops | T+1h |
| 3 | Remove the asset from owned properties; do **not** delete audience comments, and record that we did not | Digital | T+2h |
| 4 | Legal hold: briefs, approval chains, agency correspondence, research, translations, any local objection raised and overridden | Group Legal | T+2h |
| 5 | Holding line, one paragraph, published in [local language] first: *we have withdrawn it, we are listening, a fuller response follows within 24 hours from [named person]* | [Y] comms lead | T+3h |
| 6 | Brief customer-facing and retail staff in [Y] **before** any public statement — script, permission to acknowledge, escalation route, and explicit safety guidance | [Y] HR + ops | T+3h |
| 7 | Notify the top trade partners and distributors in [Y] by phone, not email | [Y] commercial lead | T+4h |
| 8 | Stand up listening: local-language monitoring, not English-language monitoring of a non-English market | Insight | T+2h |
| 9 | Freeze all campaign work in the region pending §9.2 | Regional CMO | T+4h |

**Note on #5.** The holding line commits to a time and a named person. That is deliberate. A holding statement that commits to nothing reads as a legal artefact and is treated as one.

**Note on #3.** Comment deletion is recoverable in exactly no cases and has ended several careers that the original creative would not have. We would ask that this be stated to the digital team as an instruction rather than a preference.

---

## 3. Diagnosis before design — four hours, run in parallel with §2

We would gently ask the group to test one framing before adopting it. The incident is currently described as *a cultural misunderstanding*. The evidence available to us may instead describe **a governance failure wearing cultural clothing** — and only one of those is fixed by an apology.

### 3.1 The three questions that change the response

**Q1 — Was there local objection, and was it overridden?**
Check the approval chain now, before anyone tidies it. If someone in [Y] flagged this and was overruled by the centre or by the agency, the story is no longer about a joke. It is about a company that does not listen to its own people, which is a considerably more durable and more damaging narrative — and one that will surface, because the person who raised the flag has a phone.

*If the answer is yes:* the apology must acknowledge the override without naming or exposing the individual, and §9.3 (structural remedy) moves from Month 3 to Week 2. Attempting to conceal it is the single highest-cost option available.

**Q2 — Who is actually offended, and in what proportion?**
Three distinguishable populations, easily conflated in a monitoring dashboard:

| Population | Signal | Response weight |
|---|---|---|
| Directly affected community in [Y] | Local-language, local platforms, community and religious/civic institutions, non-national-media | **Decisive** |
| Broadly sympathetic domestic public | Mainstream local media, general social | High |
| International commentary and diaspora | English-language, high volume, low local purchase | Moderate — real, but do not let it set the terms |
| Orchestrated or opportunistic actors | Coordinated timing, template language, competitor adjacency, political utility | See §4.3 |

The failure to separate these produces apologies pitched at the wrong audience — typically at international Twitter, in English, which reads in [Y] as further evidence that the market is an afterthought.

**Q3 — What exactly was the offence?**
Not "it was insensitive." Specifically: was it sacred/religious, ethnic or racial, historical or national-dignity, gender or family-role, class or caste, linguistic (a translation or transliteration error), or a matter of ritual propriety? These have materially different half-lives and materially different remedies. A translation error is repairable in a week; a perceived slight to national dignity can run for years and can attract state interest.

Have a local cultural interlocutor **outside the company** — not the agency, not an employee — describe the offence back to us in their own words within four hours. Then use *their* framing in the apology, not ours. This is the cheapest and most frequently skipped step in the entire response.

### 3.2 Severity classification

| Tier | Markers | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Local social irritation, no trade or regulator movement, decaying | Local correction, no global posture |
| 2 | National media, trade partners asking questions, government commentary absent | Posture 2, market-led (**most likely current state**) |
| 3 | Regulator or ministry engaged, retail delisting, boycott with an organised host, employee safety concerns | Posture 2 plus §12.4 escalation; Group CEO enters |
| 4 | Legal jeopardy, physical risk to staff, licence-to-operate threat | Separate protocol; this document is insufficient |

---

## 4. The calibration decision — four postures

We would ask the group to choose explicitly rather than to drift into one. Drift produces Posture 3 delivered with Posture 2 timing, which satisfies nobody.

| | Posture | When it fits | What it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Correct and continue** — fix the asset, brief note, no apology | Narrow technical error (mistranslation, wrong image credit), no dignity dimension, Tier 1 | Cheap. Fails badly if severity is misread |
| **2** | **Withdraw and apologise** — full withdrawal, unqualified apology, named accountability, structural remedy | Genuine offence to a real constituency, Tier 2–3. **Recommended** | High short-term visibility, lowest long-term cost |
| **3** | **Acknowledge and explain** — regret expressed, intent explained, asset withdrawn | Almost never. Explanation of intent reads universally as excuse | Usually generates the second cycle it seeks to avoid |
| **4** | **Hold** — withdraw quietly, decline to apologise | Genuine ambiguity **and** evidence of orchestration for commercial or political ends where concession invites escalation | High risk, occasionally correct, requires the group to accept a bad month deliberately |

### 4.1 Why we recommend Posture 2

The asymmetry is not close. An over-apology to an unoffended audience costs one news cycle and a mild internal embarrassment. An under-apology to a genuinely offended one costs a market position, and the second attempt is never believed. Given that asymmetry, we would apologise on the balance of probability rather than on proof.

### 4.2 The hedge to avoid at all costs

*"We are sorry if anyone was offended"* transfers the fault to the audience's sensitivity, is recognised as doing so in every language we are aware of, and has independently generated more coverage than the original creative in numerous comparable incidents *(judgement, though the pattern is well attested — §15)*. So has *"that was not our intent."* Intent is the brand's private property and no one else's concern. See §5.2.

### 4.3 The one circumstance in which we would counsel the group to hold its nerve

If the §3.1 Q2 analysis shows the reaction is substantially manufactured — coordinated timing, template language, a competitor or political actor with a clear interest, and **no independently locatable community objection** — then a full apology rewards the mechanism and reliably invites a repeat within the year.

We flag this not because we believe it is the current case (we do not, on present evidence), but because we would rather the group considered and rejected it in the next four hours than discovered it in six weeks. The test is falsifiable and cheap: can we find, in four hours, three credible local community or civic voices, unconnected to each other and to the campaign, who articulate the offence in their own terms? If yes, Posture 2, without further debate. If no, bring it back to the group before publishing.

---

## 5. The apology — architecture, not wording

Wording is the market's property (§7.1). Architecture is what we would ask to be fixed.

### 5.1 Eight components

| # | Component | Note |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Name the offence in the offended community's own terms** | Taken from §3.1 Q3. Using their framing is the entire signal |
| 2 | **Unconditional regret** | No "if", no "any", no "may have" |
| 3 | **Named human accountability** | A senior [Y]-based person, by name and face. Corporate voice is the voice of an entity avoiding a person |
| 4 | **What has already been done** | Past tense, verifiable, ideally completed before publishing |
| 5 | **What will change in how decisions are made** | The only forward-looking element that carries weight |
| 6 | **A date** | A public commitment to report back at 90 days |
| 7 | **A route to be answered** | A monitored channel, in language, with a response commitment |
| 8 | **Nothing else** | No product mention. No values statement. No history of our community contribution. Each addition dilutes the whole |

### 5.2 The prohibited constructions

| Phrase pattern | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| "…if anyone was offended" | Conditional; blames the audience |
| "…was not our intention" | Irrelevant; heard as excuse |
| "…does not reflect who we are" | It does; it was approved by people who work here |
| "We have always celebrated diversity…" | Invites the receipts |
| "…a learning journey" | Frames harm as our development opportunity |
| "…the actions of an individual" | Scapegoating; sequel guaranteed |
| Passive voice for the offence, active voice for the remedy | Universally noticed |

### 5.3 Form and channel

Local language first and natively written — **not translated from an English original**, which is detectable and, in this specific context, itself part of the offence. Local platforms in [Y] before global platforms. Video is warmer than text and harder to quote out of context; a plain, unproduced, single-take piece to camera outperforms a produced statement *(judgement)*. No music. No brand furniture. No grey square.

**Timing:** within 24 hours of the incident being recognised, and not on a Friday evening local time, which is read everywhere as burial.

---

## 6. Sequencing — who hears it, in what order

Almost every avoidable injury in the next fortnight is a sequencing failure rather than a content failure.

| Order | Audience | Channel | By |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Y] employees, especially customer-facing and retail | Manager cascade, in person or by voice, with a script and permission to acknowledge | Before anything public |
| 2 | Employees globally | Internal note, brief, honest, no spin | T+6h |
| 3 | Trade partners, distributors, key retail accounts in [Y] | Named-person phone calls | T+8h |
| 4 | Regulators, relevant ministries, industry bodies in [Y] | Local counsel and government affairs, in the local convention | Before media |
| 5 | Affected-community interlocutors | Private, listening posture, **no cameras, no request for absolution** | T+12–24h |
| 6 | [Y] media and public | Statement per §5 | T+24h |
| 7 | International media | Reactive only. Point them to the local statement | On enquiry |
| 8 | Other markets | Quiet brief to market leads; no proactive global publication | T+36h |

**On #5.** The single most common error is to meet community representatives and photograph it. The meeting has value; the photograph converts it into a transaction and reliably offends the people it was intended to reassure. If a record is wanted, let the community party decide whether and how to describe it.

**On #8.** We would suggest the group resist the instinct to publish a global apology. In markets where the incident has not landed, a global statement creates the awareness it seeks to manage, and the coverage will be about the apology rather than about anything else. Contain the response geographically to the extent that platform reality permits, and be honest that it permits less than it used to.

---

## 7. Authority — who decides, and what the centre binds itself to

### 7.1 The market mandate

We recommend that the Group CEO confer, in writing and visibly, a **bounded mandate** on the [Y] market MD:

> *For the next 30 days, [name] decides the content, timing, language and channel of all communications relating to this incident in [Y], and the composition of the local remedy up to a value of $[1.5]M. In a crisis paper, precise-looking numbers with no derivation invite the group to argue about the number instead of the plan. Either show a three-line build (response ops / restoration commitment / media re-entry) or present ranges.
- **Overstated absolutes.** "Recognised as doing so in every language we are aware of," "recoverable in exactly no cases," "Universally noticed," "Explanation of intent reads universally as excuse." These are good heuristics presented as laws; a single counter-example lets a sceptical executive dismiss the surrounding argument. Also "Posture 3: Almost never" is too strong — for a genuine mistranslation, factual explanation is not an excuse, it is the correction.
- **The "two-thirds of durable damage accrues after the first apology" figure** is flagged as judgement but is quantified precisely enough to be quoted back. Either source it or state it qualitatively.

**Distribution:** crisis group; [Y] market leadership team; Group Legal and local counsel; Group Communications; global media lead; regional CMO; agency of record **operational desk only** (Annex E.2 defines exactly what they receive and when). Not for wider circulation. Not external.

# PART 2 — THE FOUR DECISIONS

Each carries a **pre-selected default**. If the crisis group does not resolve a decision by the stated time, the default executes. This is deliberate: in an incident, the cost of a slightly wrong decision taken on time is almost always lower than the cost of the right decision taken late, and a group that must reach consensus before anything moves will not move.

| **D3** | Approve the response envelope and the twelve-month restoration commitment (Annex K): **$1.8–2.6M** response ops, **$5.5–7.5M** restoration over twelve months, of which the community commitment is ring-fenced and unbranded | **Approved at the mid-point**, with a T+30 review | T+12h |

We would ask the group to record any departure from a default in the decision log with a one-line reason. Not for audit — for the market. Colleagues in [Y] will accept a decision they dislike far more readily than one whose origin they cannot see.

# PART 3 — ANNEXES

## Annex A — Diagnosis: four hours, run in parallel with Part 1

We would gently ask the group to test one framing before adopting it. The incident is described as *a cultural misunderstanding*. The evidence may instead describe **a governance failure wearing cultural clothing** — and only one of those two is repaired by an apology. This distinction is the single most valuable thing in this document, and everything downstream turns on it.

### A.1 What the diagnosis must not delay
Nothing in Part 1. The diagnosis shapes the *content* of the response, not the *withdrawal*.

### A.2 Q1 — Was there local objection, and was it overridden?
Check the approval chain **now**, before anyone tidies it. If a colleague in [Y] flagged this and was overruled by the centre or by the agency, the story is no longer about a joke. It is about a company that does not listen to its own people — a far more durable and more damaging narrative, and one that will surface, because the person who raised the flag has a phone and a conscience. [P]

**If yes:** the apology acknowledges the override in general terms, without naming, quoting or exposing the individual, and without inviting the market to identify them. The structural remedy (Annex H.3) moves from Month 3 to Week 2. Concealment is the highest-cost option available to us. Annex F.2 governs how this is said without creating admissions we cannot manage.

**If we do not yet know:** say nothing about it, keep auditing, and be prepared to correct the record voluntarily and quickly. A self-corrected record costs one day. A discovered concealment costs the market.

### A.3 Q2 — Who is offended, and who determines the consequence?
Four distinguishable populations. Conflating them is what produces an apology pitched at international social media, in English, which reads in [Y] as further proof that the market is an afterthought.

| Population | Signal | Sets the *framing* | Sets the *commercial tail* |
|---|---|---|---|
| Directly affected community in [Y] | Local-language, local platforms, community, religious and civic institutions | **Decisive** | High |
| Broadly sympathetic domestic public in [Y] | Mainstream local media, general local social | High | High |
| International commentary and diaspora | English-language, high volume, low local purchase | **Low — do not let it set the words** | **High — it drives retailer risk committees, home-market employee sentiment, investor questions and regulator awareness** |
| Orchestrated or opportunistic actors | Coordinated timing, template language, competitor adjacency, political utility | None | Variable; see A.5 |

The v0.9 error was to rate international commentary "moderate" on a single axis. It is close to irrelevant for wording and close to decisive for consequence. Both statements are true at once and the response must hold both.

### A.4 Q3 — What exactly was the offence, and severity
Not "it was insensitive." Specifically: sacred or religious; ethnic or racial; historical or national dignity; gender or family role; class, caste or region; linguistic (translation or transliteration); or ritual propriety. These have materially different half-lives and materially different remedies. A transliteration error is repairable in a week. A perceived slight to national dignity can run for years and can attract state interest (Annex G.2). [P]

**Have a local cultural interlocutor from outside the company** — not the agency, not an employee — describe the offence back to us in their own words within four hours. Then use *their* framing in the apology, not ours. Cheapest step in the response; the most frequently skipped.

| Tier | Markers | Implication |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Local social irritation, no trade or regulator movement, decaying | Local correction only |
| 2 | National media, trade partners asking questions, no government commentary | Posture 2, market-led (**current assessment**) |
| 3 | Regulator or ministry engaged, delisting, organised boycott with a host, staff safety concerns | Posture 2 + Annex G.1. Group CEO enters, privately |
| 4 | Legal jeopardy, physical risk to staff, licence-to-operate threat, state amplification | Annex G.2 |

### A.5 The orchestration test — made falsifiable
v0.9 claimed a test it had not specified. Corrected:

| Element | Specification |
|---|---|
| Who runs it | Insight lead plus local counsel's public-affairs contact, **not** the agency, not the [Y] marketing team |
| Where | The three highest-reach local-language platforms in [Y], local-language search, community and religious institution channels, two local civic NGOs, one academic contact |
| What counts as a qualifying voice | Named, locatable, with a public record on the relevant issue **predating** this campaign; articulates the offence in their own terms, not in campaign-adjacent language |
| What disqualifies | Anonymous accounts; accounts created inside 90 days; template phrasing; commercial or political payment relationships; competitor connection; any voice surfaced by the agency |
| Threshold | Three qualifying voices, mutually unconnected so far as a four-hour check can establish. **We state plainly that "unconnected" cannot be verified in the window; it can only be not-disproved** |
| Adjudicator | Incident director, with a written one-paragraph finding in the decision log |

**The case v0.9 skipped, which is the usual case:** reactions that are *simultaneously* orchestrated and genuine. Amplification by an interested actor of an offence that is nonetheless real. The correct response is Posture 2, delivered locally, **without any public reference to the orchestration**. Naming amplification in public is heard as "your feelings are inauthentic," and converts a manageable incident into an insult. Note the orchestration internally, plan for recurrence (Annex H.5), say nothing.

### A.6 The withdrawal / containment tension, named
Part 1 requires global withdrawal. Annex D requires geographic containment of the *communication*. These are compatible only if stated precisely: **withdraw everywhere, announce nowhere but [Y].** A house-wide social freeze is itself visible, and trade press read media-buying pullbacks within a day, so the freeze is time-boxed at 48 hours with a T+24h review and explicit carve-outs. If asked in a third market, we confirm withdrawal factually and point to the [Y] statement. We do not proactively publish globally (Annex D.3, note on order 8).

## Annex B — The four postures

Choose explicitly. Drift produces Posture 3 delivered with Posture 2 timing, which satisfies nobody.

| | Posture | When it fits | Cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Correct and continue** — fix the asset, short factual note, no apology | Narrow technical error with no dignity dimension; Tier 1 | Cheap; fails badly if severity is misread |
| **2** | **Withdraw and apologise** — full withdrawal, unqualified apology, named accountability, structural remedy | Genuine offence to a real constituency; Tier 2–3. **Recommended** | High short-term visibility, lowest long-term cost |
| **3** | **Acknowledge and explain** — regret, withdrawal, and a factual explanation | **Narrow but real:** a demonstrable mistranslation, transliteration or production error, where the facts *are* the correction and withholding them looks evasive. Not available where dignity, sanctity or identity is engaged — there, explanation of intent is heard as excuse | Generates a second cycle whenever intent is offered in place of regret |
| **4** | **Hold** — withdraw quietly, decline to apologise | Genuine ambiguity **and** an evidenced orchestration finding under A.5 with no locatable community objection | High risk, occasionally correct, requires the group to accept a bad month on purpose |

**Why Posture 2.** The asymmetry is not close. An over-apology to an unoffended audience costs one news cycle and some internal embarrassment. An under-apology to a genuinely offended one costs a market position, and the second attempt is not believed. On that asymmetry we apologise on the balance of probability rather than on proof. [J]

**On the second cycle.** Our practitioner view, held firmly but stated qualitatively rather than as a statistic: in incidents of this kind, most of the durable damage is generated by the response, not by the original creative. v0.9 put a fraction on this. We have removed it, because a number we cannot source is a number that will be quoted back at us. [J]

---

## Annex C — The apology: architecture, not wording

Wording is the market's property under the mandate at E.1. Architecture is what we would ask the group to fix.

### C.1 Eight components
1. **Name the offence in the offended community's own terms** (from A.4). Their framing *is* the signal.
2. **Unconditional regret.** No "if", no "any", no "may have".
3. **Named human accountability** — a senior [Y]-based person, by name and face. See C.3.
4. **What has already been done** — past tense, verifiable, ideally completed before publishing.
5. **What will change in how decisions are made** — the only forward-looking element that carries weight (Annex H.3).
6. **A date** — a public commitment to report back at 90 days, kept whether or not anyone is still asking.
7. **A route to be answered** — a monitored local-language channel with a stated response commitment.
8. **Nothing else.** No product mention, no values statement, no history of community contribution. Each addition dilutes the whole.

### C.2 Constructions to avoid

| Pattern | Why it fails |
|---|---|
| "…if anyone was offended" | Conditional; transfers fault to the audience's sensitivity. We are not aware of a language in which this lands well [J] |
| "…was not our intention" | Intent is the brand's private property; offered publicly it is heard as excuse |
| "…does not reflect who we are" | It does. People who work here approved it |
| "We have always celebrated diversity…" | Invites the receipts |
| "…a learning journey" | Frames someone's harm as our development opportunity |
| "…the actions of one individual" | Scapegoating. A sequel follows |
| Passive voice for the offence, active for the remedy | Noticed far more often than drafters expect [P] |

### C.3 Accountability for the response vs attribution of cause
The distinction v0.9 blurred, and it matters:

- **Accountability for the response is named and public.** One senior [Y]-based executive puts their name and face to it and answers for what we do next.
- **Attribution of cause is never individual and never public.** The failure was a system that let the work through. Naming a copywriter, a planner or a junior marketer publicly is scapegoating, is recognised as such, and guarantees a second story. [P]

**On personnel consequences.** If the audit shows individual conduct that warrants action, it is handled privately, through the normal disciplinary process, on the normal timetable, with local employment law and any works council or union obligation observed (Annex F.3). We do not announce departures as remedy, and we do not accelerate a process to satisfy external demand. If a departure becomes public, the line is that we do not discuss individuals, and that the change we are prepared to discuss is structural (Annex H.3). Where accountability is appropriate at senior level, it is better expressed as a change in who holds sign-off than as a dismissal, because the first survives the news cycle and the second does not.

### C.4 Form, channel, timing
Local language, **natively written, not translated from an English original** — translation is detectable and in this specific context is itself part of the offence. Local platforms in [Y] before global platforms. Plain single-take video, unproduced, outperforms a produced statement. [J] No music
